video.title: I built a local model that skips YouTube sponsor reads

comment: Hand-written transcript of a plausible tech video. Two sponsor reads are labelled below; the lines around them are deliberately awkward: a subscribe/merch/Patreon block right after the first read (not sponsors), and a line about 'promo codes, free trials, links in the description' near the end that the code heuristic is allowed to get wrong but must not turn into a read.

lines.text: Today we are building something small and slightly silly: a local model that watches what you watch.
It runs on the laptop, it never calls a cloud service, and it exists because I got tired of skipping ads by hand.
The idea came from a project that does this with a hosted typed decision model, and the whole design is worth copying.
Code owns the timestamps, and the model only answers yes or no questions about a line of text that already exists.
That split is the reason this whole thing runs locally in about fourteen milliseconds per question.
So in this video I want to walk through the four pieces: captions, lines, questions and the skip itself.
By the end you will have a clear picture of where the model is useful and where plain code has to do the work.
Let me start with the way the transcript arrives, because that part surprised me the most.
Before we get to the build, a quick word about the people who made this video possible.
Today's video is sponsored by Brewmaster, the espresso machine that has replaced the office kettle for us.
It heats up in about four seconds and it grinds the beans right before the shot.
We have been using it for three months, and the crema is honestly the best part of it.
If you want one, head to brewmaster dot com slash laya and use my code LAYA20 at the checkout.
That is twenty percent off your first machine, and it also applies to the beans.
The link is in the description below, and thank you to Brewmaster for sponsoring today's video.
Anyway, back to the build. The whole idea of the project is that code owns every timestamp.
If you enjoy this kind of project, subscribe and hit the bell, it really does help the channel.
There is also a merch store now, and channel memberships, if you want the extra development logs.
Patreon supporters get the source code early, which is a nice way of saying thank you.
The first piece is the transcript. YouTube already renders captions, so we simply read them as they appear.
Each caption becomes a cue with a start time, and the cues are merged into numbered transcript lines.
A line ends when the speaker pauses, when it reaches about eleven words, or at a full stop.
Then the local model gets one question per line: is this line inside a paid read?
It answers with a probability, and the code decides what to do with that number.
Above seventy percent the line counts as inside a read, and above eighty we are willing to cut there.
The boundary is the part that matters most, because cutting a line early eats the video's own content.
So we ask about the edges separately, and then we walk backwards until the lead-in starts.
The lead-in is the story that exists only to arrive at the sponsor, and it is part of the read.
Here the whole transcript is about fifty lines, so the local model answers everything in under a second.
Let me take a quick break here and talk about the other sponsor of this video, Levelup Analytics.
It is the dashboard we use to watch how the extension behaves on real pages during the day.
You get the first month free if you sign up today with the link in the show notes.
It handles about a million events a day on their smallest plan, which is plenty for us.
Their support answered a question of ours in about ten minutes, which is why we stayed with them.
Go to levelup analytics dot io slash laya and use the code LAYA for a free upgrade.
Thank you to Levelup for sponsoring the middle of the video, and now back to the code.
Now, the part I got wrong the first time: the transcript keeps growing while you watch the video.
So the pipeline has to judge the tail again, because the last line is still being spoken.
We keep a map from line index to probability and only ask about the lines that are new.
The open read is the interesting case, because we do not know where it ends yet.
While the newest line still says yes, the video steps forward by ten seconds at a time.
As soon as two lines in a row say no, the read is closed and the end is known.
That is the same trade the audio mode upstream makes: the first seconds of a read are heard.
Everything after that is a jump that the code decided, never a guess from the model.
The panel shows every question and every probability, so you can see why it cut where it did.
If the model is missing, a small heuristic stands in, and the panel says so in the badge.
That heuristic is not clever, it just knows the phrases that only exist to sell something.
Promo codes, free trials, links in the description, and the sentences that introduce them.
It is worse than the model, and it is honest about it, which felt like the right trade.
That is the whole project. If it saved you a minute of a coffee ad, it did its job.
